title: Checkpoint: Elements Up Close
objective: After this level you can compare the properties and uses of common elements.
summary: Recycled phones yield copper, silver and gold, each chosen for its chemistry. A side-by-side table compares the chapter's conductors, change-resisters and carbon forms.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: there's a gold mine in your junk drawer.
cards.body: Old phones are packed with the elements you've just met. Recycle enough of them and the haul is real. Let's open one up, then line up the chapter's elements side by side.

cards.fact: Recycling a million phones can recover about 35 thousand pounds of copper, 772 pounds of silver and 75 pounds of gold.
cards.context: That's the EPA's count, plus a little palladium. Copper wins by weight because it's the wiring metal, second only to silver as a conductor. Gold turns up for Level 36's reason: it conducts well and doesn't react, so it's used to plate electrical contacts, terminals and printed circuits. A contact that never tarnishes keeps connecting.

cards.headline: The right element for the job

items.label: Carry current
points: Silver: the best conductor of all metals
Copper: a close second, the wiring workhorse
Silicon: a semiconductor, tuned by doping

items.label: Resist change
points: Gold: oxygen and sulfur leave it alone
Aluminum: never found as a metal in nature

items.label: Carbon's forms
points: Steel: iron with up to 2 percent carbon
Diamond: each atom bonded to four others

cards.headline: Same elements, bigger stage
cards.body: Zoom out from the phone. Hydrogen is more than 90 percent of the universe's atoms. Oxygen feeds flames and cells alike. The iron in your blood carries that oxygen, in hemoglobin. And the carbon in diamond and pencil graphite is the same element, arranged two ways. Ten levels, a handful of elements, and most of the world is already in view.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: Phones hold copper, silver and gold, each chosen for its chemistry
Silver and copper conduct best; silicon's conduction can be tuned
Gold resists change; aluminum had to be freed from rock
Hydrogen, oxygen, carbon and iron shape the universe and you

questions.prompt: By weight, which metal does recycling a million phones recover the most of?
questions.explanation: About 35 thousand pounds of copper, far more than the silver or gold, because copper is the wiring metal.

questions.prompt: Why is gold used to plate the electrical contacts inside a phone?

options.label: It is the cheapest metal available
options.rationale: Gold is expensive; it's chosen for its chemistry.

options.label: It conducts well and never tarnishes

questions.explanation: Gold conducts well and doesn't react with oxygen or sulfur, so plated contacts keep working.

questions.prompt: Elements Up Close recap: which element makes up more than 90 percent of all atoms in the universe?

options.label: Oxygen
options.rationale: Oxygen leads in Earth's crust, not the universe.

options.label: Carbon
options.rationale: Carbon builds the most compounds, but it's far less common.

options.label: Iron
options.rationale: Iron leads in Earth as a whole, not the universe.

questions.explanation: Hydrogen, the simplest element, is more than 90 percent of all atoms.

questions.prompt: Elements Up Close recap: diamond and pencil graphite are the same element. What makes them so different?

options.label: Graphite contains lead
options.rationale: Pencil "lead" has no lead in it.

options.label: Diamond is carbon mixed with silicon
How their carbon atoms are arranged
Diamond is heated graphite from a factory
options.rationale: Natural diamonds form deep in the mantle.

questions.explanation: Both are pure carbon. Diamond's atoms each bond to four others in 3D; graphite's lie in sliding sheets.

questions.prompt: Elements Up Close recap: which metal, inside hemoglobin, carries oxygen through your blood?

options.label: Copper
options.rationale: Copper's big job is carrying electric current.

options.label: Silver
options.rationale: Silver isn't part of your blood's oxygen delivery.

questions.explanation: Most of the body's iron sits in hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen from the lungs.
